full_judgment:
Mahmud Husain. C.J:— This appeal by special leave is against the judgment and order of a Bench of the High Court Division passed in an application filed by the respondent under Article 102 (2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Petition No. 254 of 1973). 

 2. The respondent was appointed District Kanungo on 5.12,56 and since then he worked for about 10 years discharging his duties we efficiency. It appears from Annexure A to the petition filed before the High Court Division that the respondent appeared for interview before the East Pakistan Public Service Commission which selected him for appointment to the East Pakistan Civil Service, (Executive Class II). Then he was appointed temporarily to the said service. Thereafter he was placed at the disposal of the Revenue Department for employment as Circle Officer (Revenue) the Gazette Notification showing his appointment runs thus:- 

 The E.P.C. S. (Executive), Class II Officers, named below are appointed to act, until further orders, as Circle Officers (Revenue) and their services are placed at disposal of the Board of Re-venue, East Pakistan, for their posting to different stations. 

 Thereafter he was released on 24.1.67 and joined his new assignment in E. P.C.S (Executive) Class II and served in the same post for about 7 years in different stations discharging his duties normally. On the 9th August 1973 he was served with an order of reversion to his previous post of District Kanango for administrative convenience. This order was challenged before the High Court division for declaring it to be illegal, malafide arbitrary, having nothing to do with any administrative necessity or convenience and his order is in fact one of reduction in rank, tutus and salary and other amenities too without any reason or jurisdiction whatsoever and that the respondent has not been given any opportunity of being heard or showing cause before issuance of such order of reversion which is rather punishment without a fair trial and arbitrarily he was condemned unheard. 

 3. The appellant submitted affidavit in opposition before the High Court contending that the respondent was appointed to the erstwhile E. P. C. S Class II temporarily and that the E. P. C. S. Class II itself is a temporary Cadre dependent upon sear to year sanction and the employment of the respondent was purely temporary. So he has got no right to hold the post substantively and as such re-version to his former post of District Kananga is not reduction in rank. The appellant denied the allegation of the respondent that the order of reversion is malafide and arbitrary, intended for victimization and that the constitutional protection against reduction in rank is not available to him. The appellant further stated that the respondent received adverse remarks from his superior officers in his annual confidential reports for the years 1967, 1968 and 1969 including bad reputation'. So the claim of the respondent that he served as a Circle Officer with great efficiency and reputation is not borne by facts. 

 4. The learned Judge of the High Court Division on due consideration of the affidavit-in-opposition and affidavit in reply declared the impugned order of reversion as one made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 5. Leave was accordingly granted to consider whether the reversion of the respondent from the purely temporary post of Circle Officer (Revenue) to his parent post as District Kanungo amounts to reduction in rank and is violative of Article 135 of the Constitution. 

 6. The learned Deputy Attorney General for the appellant contended that the cadre of E. P. C. S. (Executive) Class II was created temporarily and it is still temporary. So the question of substantive appointment of the respondent as Circle Officer (Revenue) did not arise. The respondent was reverted to his parent post for administrative convenience and it is within the competence of the Government to take such a measure within the provision] of Article 135 (2) (ii) of the Constitution and that the reversion of the respondent to his parent department did not amount to reduction in rank and that it was done for administrative convenience. So it cannot be said that the provisions of Article 135 of the Constitution have been violated. It is further contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division committed an error in interpreting the provision of Article 135 of the Constitution and erred in holding that reduction in rank covers the case of the respondent. The relevant portion of Article 135 of the Constitution is quoted below: 

 'The officers named below are appointed temporarily to the East Pakistan Civil Service (Executive) Class-II 

 So it clearly shows that the respondent was appointed for the life of the cadre itself not for a fraction of that period of the cadre. The word 'temporarily' used in Annexure 'B' cannot be attributed for classifying the respondent as temporary appointee. In our view that will be going beyond what saver is meant by Annexure 'B'. If the appellant had a desire to appoint the respondent temporarily for taking action as the like, then in that context there would have been some indication in the appointment letter itself. The appellant was invited for interview before the Public Service Commission for selection for promotion to the E. P. C. S. (Executive) Class II and the conditions given therein as will appear from Annexure 'A' to the Petition before the High Court Division do not show that the appellant would be temporary save and except that the cadre being a temporary one. Second condition of the letter was to the following effect: 

 "Any person, who is unwilling to be considered for promotion should inform the Public Service Commission of such unwillingness without any loss of time the respondent without loss of time appeared before the Public Service Commission and was appointed to the cadre. In that view of the matter it is very difficult to hold that the authority considered the appointment as temporary. The respondent understood that his appointment would continue so long the cadre remains in existence of the tenure of the cadre would not have been extended and the respondent would have been reverted to his parent post, the question of reduction in rank would not have arisen. So in our view the respondent knew it full well that he will remain in office so long as the cadre remains in existence. The affidavit-in-opposition made out a case of service record of the respondent as bad and that he received adverse remark like bad reputation, dishonesty and corruption in his Annual Confidential Reports for three years (1967, 1968 and 1969) admittedly the cadre remained in fact but the respondent has been singled out and reverted to his previous post for administrative convenience. The words administrative convenience are vague terms. The appellant in his a affidavit in opposition made out a case of bad reputation, dishonesty and corruption but these have been found to be not tenable by the learned Judges of the High Court Division. If so the plea of admin Abstractive convenience does not stand. It appears that the appellant was bent upon to take action against the respondent without any proper cause. In our view the respondent held his office substantively in the temporary cadre and he cannot be removed during the period the cadre remains in existence except for misconduct or some such mason and by following the service rules. 

 7. It appears to us that the word temporarily used in Annexure B is only because of the creation of new temporary Cadre for Provincial Civil Service, namely, East Pakistan Civil Service (Executive Class II) for manning the posts of Circle Officers (Development) and Circle Officer (Revenue) at the Thana level vide Annexure 'Y-1' (Memo No. GA VIII-206/1235 dated Dacca, the 23rd December, 1961). It was also stated therein that the strength of the cadre was provisionally fixed for 450 and this number a would be revised after the Government has been able to assess the requirement in future. It is not the case of the appellant that they have reduced the strength of the cadre at any point of time. The learned Judges of the High Court Division rightly held that Article 179 of 1962 Constitution has no corresponding Article in the Constitution of Bangladesh wherein service protection is available to both temporary and permanent employees. 

 8. The case of Chairman, Railway Board Vs. Abdul Majid DLR 1966 S.C. 532 relates to the case of a Tally Clerk who was temporarily promoted to the post of a Ticket Collector but subsequently he was reverted upheld by the Supreme Court holding that the incumbent having been temporarily promoted as Ticket Collector his reversion to his former post of a Tally Clerk did not amount to reduction in rank within the purview of Article 84 of the Constitution of 1956. It should be noted that the temporary promotion of incumbent as Ticket Collector, from the post of Tally Clerk was in consideration before the Supreme Court. In the present case the promotion was to the temporary cadre. So the respondent will rise or fall with the existence or non-existence of the cadre itself. So this case is of no assistance to the appellant. 

 9. The case of Abdul Majid Snerkn Vs. Mushaffe Ahmed and another DLR 1965 S.C. 63 relates to an incumbent appointed as a Civilian Gazetted Officer on a temporary basis and until further orders' and as such his service was protected by Article 177 of the Constitution (1962). In the present case the respondent was appointed to act 'until further orders' in a temporary cadre as Circle Officer (Revenue) and as such he is entitled to continue so long the cadre remains intact subject to the observation aforesaid. So this decision goes in favour of the respondent and not in aid of the appellant. 

 11. In the case of Hartwell Prescott Singh Vs. The Uttar Pradesh Government and other AIR 1957 SC 886 it has been held "Reversion from a temporary post held by a person does not per se amount to reduction in rank because the temporary post held by him is not his substantive rank." In that case the incumbent was appointed from time to time in a temporary capacity on probation. But in the instance the respondent was appointed and announced in service for about 7 years without break and as such when the cadre remained intact his reversion to his previous post does not amount in the circumstance of the case, to reduction in rank. So the principle enunciated in the case has no application in the facts of the present case.  The undefined duration in the appointment order of the respondent goes to show that his appointment was temporary as the cadre was temporary and not on any other Court. If there would have been a defined period in the appointment order of the respondent within the period of the tenure of the cadre then it could be said that his appointment being temporary for a particular period, his reversion to his former post would not amount to reduction in rank. The learned Judges of the High Court Division rightly held that the post of Circle Officer (Revenue) is a Gazetted one and the post of District Kanungo is a non gazetted one and the pay in the former is more than double of the pay in the latter that is Taka 225/- 500/- per month an against Taka 120-200/- per month. We find no reason for interference with the order passed by the learned Judges of the High Court Division.
